claims.claim: Photius of Constantinople (c. 810–c. 893); twice patriarch (858–867, 877–886); foremost Byzantine scholar.
The Library (Myriobiblon) summarizes/judges 279 books, pagan and Christian, many otherwise lost.
Photius was patriarch of Constantinople in 858–867 and 878–886.
Photius was born c. 820 in Constantinople and died in the 10th century or around 891.
Photius was a scholar of exceptional ability who contributed greatly to the revival of learning in the ninth century.
The Bibliotheca is a set of notes and essays which make up a record of Photius's private reading.
The work contains summaries of 279 books that Photius had read and discussed.
The Bibliotheca was written at the request of Photius's beloved brother Tarasius, who asked for summaries of works read during Photius's absence on an embassy to Assyria.
Tarasius wanted the summaries to console him for his painful separation from Photius and to acquire knowledge of works he had not yet read in their company.
Photius engaged a secretary and set down all the summaries he could recollect, arranging them in the order in which his memory recalled them rather than by subject.

In the ninth century it was still possible to read vast quantities of ancient literature, both pagan and Christian, that has since been lost, and Photius is often our best or only source of information about these lost books.
Photius was a keen critic of style and content and can be credited with taking a decisive step towards the invention of the book review.
Photius's stand on doctrinal matters brought closer the schism between Catholic and Orthodox Churches.
Photius was related through his father to Tarasius, a civil servant who was patriarch from 784 to 806, and through his mother to the empress Theodora and her brother Bardas.
